author: a. h. craven
title: Henrico County Public Library highlights Jewish American Heritage Month with reading recommendations
text:
Henrico County Public Library announced on May 27 a selection of books for all ages to mark Jewish American Heritage Month, encouraging the community to explore the culture, history, and contributions of Jewish Americans through literature. The library’s collection features recommended titles for children, teens, and adults that reflect a range of experiences and stories within the Jewish American community.
The announcement includes picture books such as “Deli Days” by Jenna Rothberg and “Something Sweet: A Sitting Shiva Story” by Lesléa Newman. For young readers, selections include “Fanny’s Big Idea: How Jewish Book Week Was Born” by Richard Michelson and “Naomi Teitelbaum Ends the World” by Samara Shanker. Teen readers are encouraged to consider titles like “The Forbidden Book” by Sacha Lamb and “Questions I Am Asked About the Holocaust” by Hédi Fried. For adults, recommendations include novels such as “The Last Woman of Warsaw” by Judith Batalion and historical works like “Crash of the Heavens: The Remarkable Story of Hannah Senesh.” Additional lists provide further options across age groups.
The library also directs those interested in learning more about heritage months to Henrico County’s Outreach and Engagement Department. In addition to its literary offerings, Henrico County Public Library enhances community life through services such as homework help, tax assistance, job search support, various meeting spaces for groups of different sizes, mobile library services to retirement facilities and day care centers, as well as facilities certified under the Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design program. The system operates nine locations throughout its service area while working to encourage reading, lifelong learning, and community enrichment by connecting people to vital information, according to the official website .
Jewish American Heritage Month is recognized nationally each May as an opportunity for communities across the United States to honor Jewish Americans’ diverse heritage.
